recent_posts.title: Introducing- Finout's MCP Integration
recent_posts.summary: Finout has launched a generally available MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes its full FinOps platform to any MCP-compatible AI client such as Claude, Copilot, or Cursor. Unlike basic cost-dashboard MCP integrations that only answer spend queries, Finout's server provides 21 tools covering anomaly detection, budget tracking, showback/chargeback, savings recommendations, commitment management, and governance. Setup is two clicks, and existing RBAC rules apply end-to-end. The announcement argues that the value of an MCP integration is bounded by the depth of the platform behind it, positioning Finout as the first MCP wired into a complete FinOps surface spanning planning, allocation, forecasting, and optimization.

recent_posts.title: Cursor pricing plans explained and 5 tips to reduce costs
recent_posts.summary: Cursor updated its pricing model in mid-2025, shifting from request-based billing to monthly usage credits, which caused user confusion and unexpected charges. The Pro plan now includes $20/month in credits for frontier models, with Auto mode usage being unlimited on paid plans. Plans range from a free Hobby tier to $200/month Ultra, plus Teams and Enterprise options. Model pricing varies significantly by provider and token type. Five cost-cutting strategies are outlined: using Auto mode by default, monitoring token consumption, limiting high-credit features like Max mode and agents, setting usage alerts, and writing concise prompts. Finout's platform is also promoted as a way to track Cursor spend alongside other cloud costs.

recent_posts.title: Yvonne Wassenaar Joins the Finout Board
recent_posts.summary: Finout, the FinOps platform used by companies like Lyft and The New York Times, announces that Yvonne Wassenaar is joining its board of directors. Wassenaar brings extensive enterprise leadership experience as former CEO of Puppet, CIO of New Relic, and current board member at Braze, JFrog, Arista Networks, and others. Simultaneously, founding board member Mat Ellis, who co-founded Cloudability and helped shape the FinOps category, is stepping down after serving since November 2022. The announcement also highlights Finout's focus on AI spend governance as the next frontier for cloud cost management.

recent_posts.title: Google Cloud Pricing Models and Examples for 11 Services [2026]
recent_posts.summary: Google Cloud uses a consumption-based pricing model with several options: pay-as-you-go, Committed Use Discounts (up to 70% off for 3-year terms), Sustained Use Discounts (up to 30% automatically applied), Spot VMs (up to 90% off), and custom enterprise agreements. Concrete pricing examples are provided for 11 services including Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Storage, VPC, Cloud CDN, Cloud SQL, Cloud Spanner, Cloud Datastore, Cloud Firestore, Bigtable, and BigQuery. The post also covers 10 cost management best practices such as using the pricing calculator, setting budget alerts, right-sizing instances, automating idle resource shutdowns, and choosing appropriate storage tiers.

recent_posts.title: How to manage AI infrastructure costs before they surprise your CFO
recent_posts.summary: As AI moves from pilot to production, organizations face a structural cost visibility problem. Panelists from Google, Shopify, and Finout discuss how to build financial discipline into AI programs from the start — including cost attribution per team and feature, unit economics tied to business outcomes, and making the CFO an active stakeholder rather than a budget gatekeeper. The core argument: teams that treat cost attribution as an engineering requirement from day one scale AI furthest and earn continued organizational investment.

recent_posts.title: Token Economics and TokenOps: The Definitive Guide to FinOps for Tokens
recent_posts.summary: TokenOps is an emerging discipline that applies FinOps principles — visibility, allocation, optimization, and governance — to LLM token consumption. As AI workloads scale, token costs can reach millions per month without proper instrumentation. The post breaks down the five layers of token spend (system prompt overhead, context/memory, model selection, output length, retry overhead), explains how to attribute costs to teams and features via tagging, and outlines optimization strategies including model tiering, semantic caching, context window management, and batch processing. A key metric introduced is 'token yield rate' — the proportion of consumed tokens that contributed to a valuable output. The post concludes with a getting-started guide covering baseline audits, mandatory tagging, unit economics metrics, and governance practices.

recent_posts.title: Snowflake pricing components explained with 2026 AI Credits update
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive breakdown of Snowflake's 2026 pricing model covering all 10 cost components: on-demand vs. capacity purchasing, regional pricing differences across AWS/Azure/GCP, virtual warehouse credit consumption (typically 60–80% of total bill), serverless feature costs, storage billing mechanics, data transfer fees, cloud services overhead, Snowpark Container Services, and the new AI Credits system introduced April 2026. The AI Credits change is the most significant update — Cortex AI features are now billed at a flat $2.00/credit regardless of edition or region, saving Business Critical customers up to 50% and VPS customers up to 79.5% on AI workloads. Includes a worked example showing ~$14,887/month for an Enterprise Edition deployment with 65TB storage, plus actionable cost control strategies like auto-suspend tuning, Time Travel retention limits, and model routing for Cortex AI.

recent_posts.title: Migrating From Cursor Teams to Enterprise: What Actually Changes, and What Catches Finance Off Guard
recent_posts.summary: Migrating from Cursor Teams to Enterprise is a fundamental shift from a per-seat SaaS subscription to a commitment contract with up to five commercial levers: annual commitment sums, committed seat counts, overage rates, pooled usage credits, and markup discounts on provider API costs. Finance teams that treat Enterprise as a scaled-up Teams plan routinely miss budget because the Admin API only exposes usage data, not contract terms like committed seats, overage rates, or prepaid credit balances. Key pitfalls include budget math still assuming per-seat pricing, undefined 'active user' contract terms, overage sticker shock during headcount growth, markup discounts obscured by shifting model prices, and broken per-user chargeback with pooled usage. Before signing, teams should nail down the active user definition, commitment vs. overage split, markup discount percentage, and termination/reallocation clauses. Post-migration tracking requires commitment-aware allocation, separation of subscription vs. on-demand costs, and real-time anomaly detection on usage pools.

recent_posts.title: FinOps for AI Agents: A Four-Step Allocation Framework
recent_posts.summary: Allocating AI agent spend (Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI, Anthropic) across engineering teams and products is fundamentally different from cloud FinOps because AI invoices arrive as consolidated line items with no per-team breakdown, costs are non-deterministic, and no taggable resource exists at the point of use. A four-step framework is proposed: centralize all AI provider invoices in a single FinOps system, replace source-level tagging with rule-based allocation, tie agent activity to developer identity (SSO/API key), and treat embedded-agent spend as product COGS. The post also outlines what to look for in a FinOps platform for AI cost management, then promotes Finout's own platform as the solution.

recent_posts.title: Why Your AI Cost Stack Is Becoming Another Reconciliation Project
recent_posts.summary: As AI spending grows rapidly, FinOps teams face a familiar problem: fragmented billing data across OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, and GPU infrastructure with no common schema or tagging model. The post argues that adding more integrations repeats the multi-cloud reconciliation mistake of 2019-2020. Instead, teams need a single system of record with unified allocation logic — including virtual tagging for untagged AI resources and native shared cost splitting — that covers cloud, Kubernetes, and AI costs together. Industry data shows 98% of organizations now manage AI spend but most still lack granular attribution, while enterprise GenAI spending tripled to $37B in 2025. The piece concludes by positioning Finout's MegaBill and Virtual Tags as the solution.
